titles: BOOK TWO. On the end of man as citizen of God's kingdom — the absolutely highest and last end, or eternal beatitude. CHAPTER ONE. Whether there is some highest good of man, and that eternal, and what it is

Every thing has its end; whatever acts tends to some good; intelligent and non-intelligent agents
4–5. Perfection and beatitude when the end is attained; the highest good defined as last and most perfect
III–IV. Perfection must be proportioned to the subject; mortal and eternal goods
Dionysius the Carthusian against Scotus; Richard on philosophers; Thomas on duplex contemplation of God
Why supernatural theology is necessary; five hypotheses before the highest good can be taught
V. The good suited to the rational immortal soul; proof that man has a rational soul
1. The rational soul is the true informing form of man — not accidental motion, crasis, or Averroist assistance
2–3. The soul is spiritual and separable from matter; VI hypotheses for teaching the highest good
VII. Immortality of the soul defined; Bernard, Nyssenus, Augustine, Ambrose on death as change — Cap. 1 close
